clue.text: Vacuous drive to plug identical articles from a certain range

indicators.note: a plug is stuffed into a gap, so these letters go inside the pair of articles

parts.note: first of two identical indefinite articles

indicators.note: vacuous means empty, so the word drive loses its inside and keeps only its shell

parts.note: the first and last letters of drive
the second of the matching pair

explanation.surface: A spaced-out motorist slots matching items into a range of products.
explanation.walkthrough: The empty drive sits between AN and AN to make ANDEAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Andean describes things belonging to the Andes, the South American mountain range, so 'from a certain range' fits the adjective.

clue.text: Adam, as described by George, is a venerable fellow

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the surname of the title hero of George Eliot's novel Adam ...
second meaning: the Anglo-Saxon monk and historian known as the Venerable

explanation.surface: A man called Adam, as a friend called George portrays him, is a grand old chap.
explanation.walkthrough: George is George Eliot, the pen name of Mary Ann Evans; 'venerable' is the title always attached to the eighth-century monk BEDE.
explanation.definitionFit: The same surname belongs to Eliot's fictional carpenter and to the historian monk styled 'the Venerable'.

clue.text: Yet to fill beaker, oddly, or jug in France

indicators.note: filling a vessel means putting something inside it, so one piece sits within the other
oddly asks for the letters in odd-numbered positions of the word beside it

parts.note: first and third letters of beaker, the start of its odd letters
yet and still both mean nevertheless
the fifth letter, last of the odd letters

explanation.surface: A lab instruction about filling a beaker, or a French jug.
explanation.walkthrough: Beaker's odd letters BAE are filled with STILL. Jug is slang for prison; the Bastille was the Paris prison stormed in 1789.
explanation.definitionFit: Jug is informal for prison, and the Bastille was the famous state prison in Paris, so it is a French jug.

clue.text: Breaches of the peace reportedly leading to sentence

indicators.note: reportedly means as it is said or heard, so the sound of the word counts, not its spelling

parts.note: frays are brawls or scuffles, breaches of the peace

explanation.surface: Public disorder offences end with a prison sentence being handed down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sentence' looks like a court penalty but is the grammatical sense. Frays and PHRASE sound the same.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrase is a group of words, loosely a sentence or expression, so the grammatical sense of sentence matches it.

clue.text: Say I do understand problem of French revolutionary

indicators.note: something revolutionary turns right round, so the French word is read from end to start

parts.note: to get something is to understand it
a hitch is a snag or problem
de is French for of, turned round

explanation.surface: Someone claims to grasp the difficulty of a French radical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say I do' reads as an assertion, but it is the definition: the words spoken at a wedding.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'I do' is the vow at a wedding ceremony, so to say it is to marry, informally to get hitched.

clue.text: Supply ale or gin in local

indicators.note: supply as an adverb means in a supple, bendy way, so the letters are flexed into a new order

parts.note: the eight letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Stock beer or gin at the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Local' tempts as the British word for one's nearest pub, but here it is an adjective; 'Supply' is supple-ly, not provide.
explanation.definitionFit: Regional and local both describe something confined to a particular area rather than the whole country.

clue.text: Pained look of red maybe bored by Conservative

indicators.note: something bored by a drill has a hole made through its middle, so a letter goes inside

parts.note: red is an example of a wine
C is the standard abbreviation for Conservative

explanation.surface: A bored Tory gives a pained look at a glass of red.
explanation.walkthrough: C goes into WINE to make WINCE.
explanation.definitionFit: A wince is a brief grimace of pain or embarrassment, a pained facial expression.

clue.text: One with large bill from court, where defendant is smuggling cocaine

parts.note: to court someone is to woo them

indicators.note: a smuggler carries goods hidden inside, so the drug letter is tucked within the dock word

parts.note: the dock is where the accused stands in a criminal court
C is slang for cocaine

explanation.surface: A drug smuggler in the dock faces a hefty bill from the court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a legal invoice, and 'court' a law court, but the bill is a beak and court is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The woodcock is a wading bird with a notably long straight beak, so it has a large bill.

clue.text: People with successful records long to include one short snippet of song

indicators.note: to include something is to take it inside, so a letter sits within the word for long

parts.note: to ache for something is to long for it
Roman numeral one

indicators.note: short means cut off before the end, so the snippet loses its final letter

parts.note: a verse is a section of a song

explanation.surface: Chart-topping musicians are keen to slip in a brief bit of a song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Records' sounds like discs but means track records of success; 'long' is the verb, to yearn.
explanation.definitionFit: Achievers are people who accomplish things, so they have records of success behind them.

clue.text: Brief answer received by staff in commercial channel

parts.note: a silk is a senior barrister, and a brief is slang for a lawyer

indicators.note: something received by a holder is taken in, so the letter goes inside the word for staff

parts.note: a rod is a staff or stick
A is the usual abbreviation for answer

explanation.surface: A short reply is taken by employees in a TV shopping channel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brief' looks like an adjective meaning short, but it is a lawyer. A silk is a King's Counsel in Britain, so called from the silk gown. A goes into ROD.
explanation.definitionFit: The Silk Road was the ancient network of trade routes between China and the West, a channel of commerce.

clue.text: Open boxes are behind electronic stuff

indicators.note: to box something is to enclose it, so the next letters are put inside

parts.note: overt means open, not hidden

indicators.note: behind means coming after, so the word for are follows the electronic letter

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for electronic, as in e-mail
an are is a metric unit of area, abbreviated A

explanation.surface: An open box sits behind the electrical goods.
explanation.walkthrough: E then A go inside OVERT. 'Stuff' looks like a noun for goods, but it is the verb, to stuff oneself.
explanation.definitionFit: To stuff yourself is to eat too much, which is what overeat means; both are verbs.

clue.text: A source of cash keeps personnel excited

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it inside, so the staff letters sit within the cash source

parts.note: a till is a cash register, where money comes from in a shop
HR is human resources, the personnel department

explanation.surface: A cash machine holds the staff in a state of excitement.
explanation.walkthrough: HR, human resources, is the modern name for a personnel department.
explanation.definitionFit: To be all a-thrill is to be thrilled, tingling with excitement, so the predicative adjective matches excited.

clue.text: Dishonest about dodgy rental housing feature

indicators.note: about means around, so the word for dishonest wraps the other letters

parts.note: cheating means behaving dishonestly

indicators.note: dodgy means unreliable or not right, so the letters are not in the right order

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A crooked landlord's shady letting of property.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Housing' looks like accommodation to rent, but it is a house, and the feature is something installed in one.
explanation.definitionFit: Central heating is a system that warms a whole building, a standard feature of a house.

clue.text: On Spotify perhaps, better pay rate again

parts.note: re means on or concerning
Spotify is an example of an app, an application
a raise is an increase in pay

explanation.surface: Musicians argue that streaming services should pay a higher rate.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface splits as 'better pay rate'; the cryptic split is 'better pay' then 'rate again'.
explanation.definitionFit: To reappraise is to assess or value something afresh, which is to rate it a second time.

clue.text: Reading fans heckle the number 4 of Stoke FC?

parts.note: to boo is to jeer or heckle

indicators.note: the number four of a word is its fourth letter, as a shirt number names one player in a team

parts.note: the fourth letter of Stoke
FC stands for Football Club

explanation.surface: Supporters of Reading jeer the number four shirt at Stoke City.
explanation.walkthrough: Reading and Stoke are both English football clubs, which sets the misleading scene; Reading is the hobby, read with a capital to hide it.
explanation.definitionFit: A book club is a group of people who meet to discuss books, so its members are fans of reading.

clue.text: Boldness about the time we live in

parts.note: c is short for circa, Latin for about
our age is the period we live in

explanation.surface: Daring is the theme of the present era.
explanation.walkthrough: C plus OUR AGE spells COURAGE.
explanation.definitionFit: Courage is bravery, the quality of being bold in the face of danger.

clue.text: Wanting weapons to protect hotel safe

indicators.note: to protect something is to surround and shield it, so the letter is held inside

parts.note: lacking weapons is being unarmed
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone wants guns to guard a hotel's strongbox.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Safe' looks like a noun, a strongbox, but it is the adjective. H goes inside UNARMED.
explanation.definitionFit: Unharmed means uninjured, and safe in the sense of having come through without hurt.

clue.text: Moor boat, regularly going "ahoy there!"

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter of the word is taken

parts.note: the second and fourth letters of boat
ahoy there is a greeting, as hello is

explanation.surface: Tie up the boat, calling out a sailor's greeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moor' looks like a verb, to tie up a boat, but it is the noun: Shakespeare's Othello is the Moor of Venice.
explanation.definitionFit: Othello is the title character of Shakespeare's tragedy, a Moorish general known as the Moor of Venice.

clue.text: Prepares to reproduce fancy vase, out to mould 50

indicators.note: fancy means elaborate or fanciful, so the letters are rearranged into something new
moulding reshapes material, so these letters too are worked into the mix

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: A potter gets ready to copy an ornate vase, putting fifty out to set.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reproduce' suggests making a copy of the vase; it means biological reproduction.
explanation.definitionFit: To ovulate is to release an egg from the ovary, the step that readies a body for conception.

clue.text: Male assistant with Nixon, say, pocketing cash to create scandal for Kennedy

indicators.note: to pocket something is to tuck it inside, so the money word goes into the pair around it

parts.note: a chap is a man
a PA is a personal assistant
quid is British slang for a pound
Richard Nixon was nicknamed Tricky Dick; Dick is short for Richard

explanation.surface: A Nixon aide taking a bribe sounds like a political scandal, though the clue pins it on a Kennedy.
explanation.walkthrough: The cash lands between the assistant and Nixon. Chappaquiddick is the island where Senator Ted Kennedy drove off a bridge in 1969, killing his passenger.
explanation.definitionFit: The Chappaquiddick incident, a fatal 1969 car crash, became the scandal that dogged Ted Kennedy's political career.

clue.text: Upset, handle cross American feller

indicators.note: upset means tipped over, and in a down clue that turns the letters to read bottom to top

parts.note: a handle is slang for a name
an X is a cross
A is the abbreviation for American

explanation.surface: An irritated American picks up an angry cross.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole run NAME, X, A is turned round. 'Feller' looks like slang for a fellow; it is one who fells trees.
explanation.definitionFit: An axeman chops down trees with an axe, so he is literally a feller, one who fells.

clue.text: Running or quarrelling?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: consecutively, as in three days running
second meaning: engaged in an argument, a row

explanation.walkthrough: Row has two pronunciations: one rhymes with go and means a line, the other rhymes with cow and means a quarrel.
explanation.definitionFit: Running means one after another, consecutively; to be in a row with someone is to be arguing with them.

clue.text: It may be used when charming women turned up make-up

definitions.text: It may be used when charming

parts.note: W is the abbreviation for women

indicators.note: turned up in a down clue means flipped to read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: DNA is one's genetic make-up

explanation.surface: Women apply cosmetics when trying to be charming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make-up' suggests cosmetics but is genetic make-up. 'Charming' is casting a charm, as a magician does.
explanation.definitionFit: A wand is the stick a magician or witch waves when casting a spell, which is charming in the magical sense.

clue.text: Decked in expensive material, scoffed about waste product

indicators.note: about means around, so the word for scoffed wraps the next one

parts.note: to scoff is to eat greedily
urea is a waste compound excreted in urine

explanation.surface: Someone dressed in finery mocks a by-product of industry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scoffed' suggests mocked but means ate greedily.
explanation.definitionFit: Aureate means golden or gilded, from Latin aurum, gold, so it is covered in a costly material.

clue.text: Great trouble concealing jollies in high-flying post

indicators.note: to conceal something is to hide it inside, so the marines go within the other letters

parts.note: A1 means first-rate, written AI in crosswords
a jolly is old slang for a Royal Marine, abbreviated RM
to ail is to trouble or afflict

explanation.surface: Serious difficulties hide fun outings at a high-powered job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jollies' looks like fun trips but is old slang for Royal Marines; 'Great' is A1, first-rate.
explanation.definitionFit: Airmail is post carried by aircraft, so it literally flies high, a play on high-flying meaning ambitious.

clue.text: See 9
Voyager's here with two velocities going in different directions

indicators.note: two things heading different ways means one of them runs backwards against the other

parts.note: speed is velocity, the first of the two
pace is velocity, the second of the two, read forwards

explanation.surface: A traveller arrives with two speeds heading opposite ways.
explanation.walkthrough: Voyager is the NASA space probe launched in 1977, now beyond the solar system.
explanation.definitionFit: The Voyager probes have travelled out past the planets into interstellar space, so deep space is where they are.

clue.text: Scientific feat from medic tracking blood types

indicators.note: tracking means following behind, so the medic comes after the other letters

parts.note: A, B and O are blood groups, together the ABO system
MB is Bachelor of Medicine, a doctor's qualification

explanation.surface: A doctor's study of blood groups is a scientific breakthrough.
explanation.walkthrough: The atomic bomb from the Manhattan Project is the feat; 'medic' gives the doctor's degree, Bachelor of Medicine.
explanation.definitionFit: The atomic bomb was a landmark, if grim, achievement of twentieth-century physics.
